strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated NLP problem: training-free multi-attribute controllable summarization, where attribute interactions make one-shot prompting unreliable.

The core idea of casting attribute control order as a planning problem with summary-level MCTS nodes is sensible and technically coherent, and the method is described with enough algorithmic detail, prompts, hyperparameters, and hardware information to support partial reproducibility.

Experiments cover multiple datasets, model families, and model sizes, and results consistently show improved automatic controllability metrics over direct prompting, self-planning prompts, and a fine-tuned HP+SP baseline.

The analysis sections add useful evidence: ablations over local reward versus heuristic scoring, control-frequency visualizations, attribute weighting experiments, and runtime measurements clarify when and why the method helps.

The method preserves ROUGE/BERTScore roughly near baseline levels while substantially improving deterministic controls such as length and specificity, which supports the claim that controllability gains do not obviously collapse general summary quality.
weaknesses: The evaluation is heavily tied to the same automatic attribute measurements used for search and final selection, creating a risk of metric overfitting; the paper does not sufficiently validate whether improved control scores correspond to genuinely better user-perceived summaries.

There is no human evaluation of controllability, relevance, factuality, coherence, or preference, despite the paper making claims about user alignment and summary quality. ROUGE and BERTScore are weak evidence for these aspects.

Factual consistency and content preservation are under-evaluated. Iterative rewriting can introduce omissions or hallucinations, but the experiments do not include factuality metrics or manual error analysis.

The main comparisons are somewhat limited: self-planning baselines appear weak, HP+SP is an older fine-tuned encoder-decoder baseline, and stronger inference-time baselines such as best-of-N sampling, iterative refinement without MCTS, constrained decoding where applicable, or budget-matched search variants are missing.

The computational cost is large: PACO takes about 196 seconds per 70B summary, far more than baselines. The paper acknowledges this but does not provide a convincing efficiency analysis under equal inference budgets.

The novelty is incremental rather than transformative: applying MCTS/planning to iterative LLM refinement is natural given recent tree-search-for-LLMs work, though the summary-level formulation and attribute-control framing are useful.

Some methodological details remain underspecified for exact reproduction, including dataset split sizes used in experiments, decoding parameters, how probabilities for the heuristic Yes/No score are obtained across models, and whether all outputs/code will be released.

The final decision rule selects the node with highest degree across the entire tree rather than using standard MCTS statistics, which may work empirically but weakens the interpretation of MCTS as the decisive mechanism; more ablations against simpler exhaustive or greedy revision policies are needed.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and practical NLP problem: controlling several summary attributes simultaneously without per-attribute fine-tuning.
The proposed summary-level MCTS framing is clearly motivated and reasonably explained, with prompts, hyperparameters, and algorithmic details included in the appendix.
Experiments cover multiple datasets, domains, and model scales, and the reported automatic controllability metrics consistently improve under PACO, especially for length and specificity.
The paper includes useful analyses of attribute-control frequency, step-wise behavior, value-function ablations, and runtime cost.
weaknesses: The evaluation is partly circular: PACO searches using essentially the same automatic attribute metrics that are later reported as controllability gains. This makes the central claim less convincing unless supported by independent human evaluation or held-out criteria.

The automatic attribute metrics are weak proxies for user-specified controllability and quality. Specificity as named-entity ratio, extractiveness as word overlap, and topic/speaker BERTScore can be gamed, and the paper does not show that optimized summaries remain faithful, useful, or semantically adequate.

Baselines are incomplete for isolating the value of MCTS. The paper lacks compute-matched comparisons such as greedy iterative repair, random/beam attribute-order search, best-of-N candidate selection, or exhaustive shallow search. Since final selection chooses the highest-scoring node from many generated candidates, some gains may come from extra inference and metric-based reranking rather than planning.
The method is expensive: PACO is reported as much slower than baselines, but the paper does not provide a careful quality-control tradeoff curve over simulations, depth, or equal runtime budgets.

The MCTS formulation has underspecified or questionable components. The policy prior pi_theta(s,a) is not clearly defined, all actions remain legal, the heuristic value is ineffective, and the final decision ignores standard visit/value criteria by selecting the highest degree anywhere in the tree. This weakens the claim that the contribution is specifically an effective MCTS planning method.

Summary quality evidence is limited to ROUGE and BERTScore, with no human preference, factual consistency, coherence, or relevance evaluation. This is particularly important because iterative attribute editing can easily remove important content or introduce distortions.

Reproducibility is only partial. Prompts and some hyperparameters are provided, but key details such as sample sizes, decoding parameters, implementation/code availability, statistical significance, and exact evaluation settings are missing or unclear.

The novelty over iterative controllable summarization plus search/reranking is moderate. The paper would need stronger empirical isolation and independent validation to support main-conference acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant NLP problem: multi-attribute controllable summarization where constraints interact and single-pass prompting is unreliable.

The proposed PACO framework is technically sensible: summary-level MCTS nodes keep the search space manageable, actions correspond naturally to attribute-specific revisions, and the method supports revisiting attributes when later edits disturb earlier controls.

Empirical results are consistently positive across MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, and DialogSum, and across 1B, 7B, and 70B models. The gains on deterministic controls such as length, extractiveness, and specificity are substantial, while summary quality metrics remain broadly comparable to baselines.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main tables, including comparisons to implicit/explicit self-planning, plan-frequency visualizations, value-function ablations, attribute-weight sensitivity, prompts, hyperparameters, and runtime measurements.
The method is training-free and practically appealing for adapting to new attribute combinations without attribute-specific fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The evaluation is heavily tied to automatic attribute metrics that are also used in the search reward, so the strongest evidence partly measures optimization of the authors' own scoring functions rather than independently validated human-perceived controllability or usefulness.

There is no human evaluation of summary quality, factual consistency, coherence, or whether the controlled outputs remain faithful to the source. ROUGE and BERTScore are insufficient to rule out quality degradation or hallucination under iterative editing.

The computational cost is high: PACO takes about 196 seconds per 70B summary, substantially slower than already expensive self-planning baselines. The paper acknowledges this but does not provide enough analysis of cost-quality tradeoffs, budget scaling, or lower-cost variants.

The baseline set is reasonable but not fully convincing for isolating the value of MCTS. Stronger test-time search baselines such as random/control-order search, beam over attribute orders, greedy best-improvement editing, or fixed-order iterative refinement would better establish that MCTS itself is the decisive component.

Some methodological details remain underspecified for reproducibility, including decoding settings, exact sample sizes/splits, significance testing, implementation details for probability extraction in the heuristic score, and whether code/model outputs will be released.

The novelty is moderate rather than exceptional: applying MCTS-style planning to attribute revision is a good fit and well executed, but the conceptual move builds directly on existing LLM tree-search and iterative controllable summarization ideas. This limits confidence in a clear main-conference recommendation despite the paper's soundness.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated NLP problem: multi-attribute controllable summarization without attribute-specific fine-tuning. Recasting control as sequential attribute planning is a sensible framing for correlated constraints such as length, extractiveness, specificity, topic, and speaker focus.

The proposed PACO framework is clearly described at a high level, with a concrete MCTS-style procedure, summary-level nodes, repeated attribute actions, reward definitions, prompts, hyperparameters, and hardware details provided in the appendix.

The experimental section is broader than many papers in this area: results cover multiple datasets/domains, three LLM backbones of different sizes, trained and prompting baselines, self-planning variants, computation-matched iterative baselines, and an ablation of the value function.

The main empirical trend is reasonably consistent: PACO improves deterministic attribute control, especially length, across datasets and model sizes, while usually preserving ROUGE/BERTScore at roughly comparable levels.

The paper includes useful analyses of control-plan distributions, attribute-control frequencies, value-function choices, and the tradeoff between deterministic and non-deterministic attribute weights.
weaknesses: The central claims are somewhat overstated. PACO does not uniformly improve all attributes: topic and speaker scores are often essentially tied with or below the base model, and the strongest gains are concentrated in deterministic metrics, especially length.

The evaluation is partly circular: PACO searches and selects summaries using the same automatic attribute measurements used for reporting. This supports metric optimization, but it gives weaker evidence that the summaries satisfy user intent in a human-meaningful way, especially for topic and speaker focus.

The evidence for preserved summary quality is limited. ROUGE and BERTScore are weak proxies for factuality, coherence, relevance, and readability, and no human evaluation or factual consistency metric is reported despite repeated claims about maintaining quality.

The MCTS contribution is less decisive than presented. The ablation shows the heuristic value function adds little, and random sequential or joint iterative baselines are competitive in several settings, so the benefit over simpler search-and-rerank procedures appears modest rather than transformative.

Several methodological details are underspecified for reproducibility and interpretation: the exact evaluation split/sample sizes are not clear in the extracted text, statistical significance is not reported, random seeds/variance are absent, and the definition or computation of the PUCT prior policy πθ(s,a) is unclear.

The computation-cost discussion is not fully convincing. PACO is substantially slower than self-planning baselines, and the computation-matched baselines are matched by number of generations rather than clearly by wall-clock cost or model calls including scoring overhead.

The comparison to trained baselines is somewhat uneven: HP+SP is based on BARTlarge and prior-style supervision, whereas PACO uses modern instruction-tuned LLMs with precise numeric prompts. This is informative but does not isolate the value of the proposed planning method.

The paper would benefit from stronger error analysis showing when sequential control harms content selection, factuality, or fluency, since repeated summary rewriting can plausibly introduce omissions or distortions.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant ACL/NLP problem: multi-attribute controllable summarization without per-attribute fine-tuning. The framing of attribute control as sequential refinement is reasonable and practically motivated.
The method is evaluated across several datasets and model scales, including MACSumDial, MACSumDoc, and DialogSum, and includes comparisons to fine-tuned and prompting-based baselines.
The appendix provides prompts, major hyperparameters, hardware information, and a computational-cost table, which helps partially assess reproducibility.
The budget-matched comparisons against joint-iterative and random sequential methods are a useful attempt to separate search structure from additional inference compute.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated. PACO often optimizes and selects outputs using essentially the same automatic attribute metrics used for evaluation, so the reported controllability gains may partly reflect metric-directed best-of-search rather than robust human-relevant control.

The MCTS formulation is not fully convincing. The policy prior in PUCT is underspecified, the final decision simply selects the highest-degree node across the whole tree, and the method often resembles metric-guided iterative refinement rather than a principled MCTS planner. Claims about discovering optimal control paths are therefore not well supported.

The strongest comparisons do not decisively establish the value of PACO. Budget-matched random sequential and joint-iterative baselines are often close to PACO, especially for deterministic attributes, so the incremental benefit of the customized tree search is smaller than the narrative suggests.

Evaluation of summary quality is weak. ROUGE and BERTScore are insufficient to show that factuality, coherence, relevance, and user satisfaction are preserved, especially when summaries are repeatedly rewritten to satisfy surface constraints.
The paper claims alignment with user preferences but provides no human evaluation, preference study, or task-based user evidence. This is a substantial gap given the stated motivation.

The non-deterministic attributes are problematic: topic and speaker scores are near-saturated, sometimes decrease under PACO, and are measured with embedding similarity metrics whose validity for the intended controls is not carefully justified.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. Important details such as dataset splits/sample sizes, exact model serving settings, random seeds, statistical significance, and implementation details for search bookkeeping are not sufficiently specified.

The computational overhead is large: PACO is roughly 196 seconds per summary for the 70B model, much slower than baselines. The paper acknowledges this but does not adequately analyze whether the quality/control gains justify the cost in realistic settings.

Some baselines appear weak or disadvantaged. The self-planning prompts perform worse than the base model, raising questions about prompt design rather than demonstrating a fundamental limitation of LLM planning.

Presentation quality is uneven, with several grammatical issues and overclaiming throughout. Figures also appear visually hard to read in extraction, and some terminology such as deterministic/non-deterministic attributes is not explained with enough rigor.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical NLP problem: multi-attribute controllable summarization without attribute-specific fine-tuning. The framing of summary-level MCTS as sequential attribute revision is clear and well motivated by the interactions among length, extractiveness, specificity, topic, and speaker focus.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad, covering multiple datasets/domains and several model scales, including 1B, 7B, and 70B instruction-tuned LMs. PACO shows consistent improvements on deterministic control metrics, especially length and specificity, and the gains hold beyond a single backbone.

The paper includes useful comparisons against LLM self-planning and computation-matched iterative/random baselines, which helps separate the benefit of structured search from simply spending more inference calls.

The appendices provide prompts, hyperparameters, algorithmic details, ablations of the value function, attribute-weighting analysis, and runtime measurements, making the method more reproducible than many inference-time LLM papers.

The contribution is conceptually simple but effective: summary-level nodes keep the search space tractable, and allowing attributes to be revisited is well suited to the non-monotonic nature of multi-attribute revision.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is partly circular: PACO selects nodes using the same or very similar automatic attribute measurements that are later reported as controllability metrics. This supports optimization of those metrics, but weakens claims about satisfying real user preferences or true semantic control.

Summary quality is evaluated only with ROUGE and BERTScore, which are insufficient for the claimed preservation of quality. There is no human evaluation or factuality/consistency assessment, even though iterative rewriting could introduce omissions, hallucinations, or degraded coherence.

The paper’s strongest claims about adaptive planning and discovering optimal control orders are somewhat overstated. Since the final summary is chosen by the highest measured degree over the explored tree, the method can also be viewed as metric-guided search/reranking rather than evidence of genuinely optimal planning.

Some methodological details remain underspecified or confusing for reproducibility, including the exact definition and scaling of the final degree score, the action prior pi_theta in PUCT, epsilon, dataset sample sizes/splits used for LLM experiments, random seeds, and how chat-model beam search is implemented.

The baselines are helpful but not exhaustive. The fine-tuned HP+SP baseline is based on an older BART setup, and stronger recent test-time optimization, constrained decoding, reranking, or edit-based controllable summarization baselines would make the comparison more convincing.

The computational cost is substantial: PACO is reported to take about 196 seconds per 70B summary, far slower than the base model and self-planning baselines. The paper acknowledges this but does not deeply analyze the tradeoff or provide an efficient variant with comparable performance.

The presentation has several minor clarity and formatting issues in figures/tables and prose, and some claims such as “strong alignment with user preferences” are not directly supported by the evidence presented.
